name: Treaty with the Coast Tribes of Oregon, 1855 (unratified Coast Treaty)
aka: Treaty of 1855 with the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw (unratified)
citation: Never ratified; published in Senate Executive Document No. 25, 53rd Congress, 1st session
promises: The bands would cede their lands on the Oregon coast in return for money payments.
A reservation would be created for them within the ceded area.
The treaty was to take effect only on ratification by the United States.

breaches.what: The treaty Superintendent Joel Palmer concluded with the coast tribes on August 11, 1855 was not sent to the Senate until February 1857 and was never ratified.

breaches.quote: It was not submitted to the Senate until February, 1857, and was never ratified.

breaches.what: Royce's land cession schedule, published by the Smithsonian's Bureau of American Ethnology, records that Palmer's 1855 coast treaties were not ratified but that United States authorities treated the cession as binding, set apart the promised reservation by Executive Order of November 9, 1855, and mapped the cession as though ratified.

breaches.quote: The treaties were not ratified, but the U. S. authorities assumed that the cession was binding

breaches.what: The Supreme Court upheld the Court of Claims finding that the Tillamook, Coquille, Tututni and Chetco were deprived of their original Indian title by the Executive Order of November 9, 1855 without consent or compensation, the Tillamook confined to part of their land and the others moved to the Coast (Siletz) Reservation, and held they could recover.

breaches.what: The Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw say they agreed to the 1855 treaty and waited in vain for ratification, that the government chose to ignore it, and that within a year they were rounded up and held at Fort Umpqua, then marched in 1860 to the Alsea subagency, where half their people died.

landTaken: Royce's Area 397 on the Oregon coast, treated by the United States as ceded although the treaty was never ratified (Royce, 1899).
compensation: The Tillamook, Coquille, Tututni and Chetco recovered for the taking after the 1946 ruling; the amount was not recorded in this pass. An earlier suit by the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw, under a jurisdictional act worded like the 1935 Act, was denied in 1938 because original Indian title had not been proved (Coos Bay, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indian Tribes v. United States, 87 Ct. Cl. 143, as described in Alcea).
today: The Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw were terminated in 1954 over their opposition and restored by Public Law 98-481 on October 17, 1984 (CTCLUSI, History).

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians
nationVoice.summary: The Tribes say they kept their side of the 1855 treaty, the government ignored it, and federal promises of just treatment were persistently broken for the next hundred years.

plain.promised: Money payments for the bands' lands on the Oregon coast, and a reservation for them within the ceded area, once the treaty was ratified.
plain.happened: The treaty went to the Senate only in February 1857 and was never ratified, yet the United States treated the land as ceded. In 1946 the Supreme Court upheld a finding that the Tillamook, Coquille, Tututni and Chetco lost their land without consent or payment.
plain.today: Those four tribes recovered for the taking; the amount has not been traced. A 1938 suit by the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw was denied. Those tribes were terminated in 1954 and restored in 1984.

openQuestions: Royce describes 'several treaties' concluded with the coast tribes between August 11 and September 8, 1855; which bands signed which instrument was not sorted out here, and the cession entries dated November 9, 1855 in treaties.json may cover the same lands.
The amount recovered by the Tillamook and other bands after 1946 (and the later Indian Claims Commission dockets 239 and 240 for Tillamook and Clatsop bands) was not recorded.
The treaty text in Senate Executive Document No. 25, 53rd Congress, was not opened.
The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians and the Coquille Indian Tribe were not consulted for their own accounts in this pass.

Audit 2026-11-08: compensation no longer says the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw were excluded from the 1935 Act; Alcea (329 U.S. 40) says only that their 1938 suit, under an earlier act in identical language, failed for want of proof of original title.
Status set to broken on 2026-11-08 under Jordan's rule: never ratified, but the land was taken and a finding documents it. The never-ratified breach stays so the map labels it.
